items.followUp: A vector of magnitude 10 N makes an angle of 30° with the horizontal. Find its horizontal and vertical components.

rubric.why: The vector is resolved into components along two perpendicular axes.
rubric.description: Identifies the two rectangular components and their values.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for both component formulas, with the horizontal component using cosine and the vertical component using sine.

rubric.why: Rectangular components act along perpendicular directions.
rubric.description: States that the components are at right angles to each other.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the components are perpendicular or at 90°.

modelAnswer: The rectangular components of a vector are its components along two mutually perpendicular directions, usually the horizontal and vertical axes.
If a vector of magnitude A makes an angle θ with the horizontal, its horizontal component is Ax = A cos θ and its vertical component is Ay = A sin θ.
Their values depend on the magnitude of the vector and the angle it makes with the axes.

items.followUp: Give an example of a body moving with constant velocity while in equilibrium, and state why it is in equilibrium.

rubric.why: A body moving at constant velocity has zero acceleration and can be in dynamic equilibrium.
rubric.description: Gives a valid example of a moving body in equilibrium.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for an example such as a raindrop or parachutist falling at terminal velocity.

rubric.why: Equilibrium requires the resultant force on the body to be zero.
rubric.description: States the condition that makes the example an equilibrium case.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the forces are balanced or the net force is zero.

modelAnswer: A parachutist falling at terminal velocity is moving but is in equilibrium.
The air resistance balances the weight, so the resultant force is zero and the parachutist moves with constant velocity.

items.followUp: What is neutral equilibrium? Give two examples of bodies in neutral equilibrium.

accept: height of centre of gravity remains unchanged
centre of gravity remains at the same height
rubric.why: In neutral equilibrium, a small displacement does not change the height of the centre of gravity.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that after displacement the body neither returns nor moves farther away, or that its centre of gravity remains at the same height.

rubric.why: These are standard examples of neutral equilibrium.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for two valid examples, such as a ball on a horizontal surface and a cylinder rolling on a horizontal surface.

modelAnswer: A body is in neutral equilibrium if, when displaced slightly, it neither tends to return to its original position nor moves farther away; its centre of gravity remains at the same height.
Examples are a ball on a horizontal surface and a cylinder rolling on a horizontal surface.

items.followUp: A truck and a car move at the same speed. Which has greater kinetic energy, and why?

rubric.why: Kinetic energy depends on both mass and the square of speed.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that kinetic energy is proportional to mass and the square of speed, or writing the formula.

rubric.why: A car has much greater mass than a motorcycle, which can outweigh the motorcycle's speed advantage.
rubric.description: Explains how the slow-moving car can have more kinetic energy.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that the car's much larger mass can give it greater kinetic energy despite its lower speed.

modelAnswer: Kinetic energy is given by KE = ½mv², so it depends on mass as well as the square of speed.
A car has much greater mass than a motorcycle; therefore, even at a lower speed, its kinetic energy may be greater.

items.followUp: A person pushes a wall but it does not move. Is work done on the wall? Explain.

rubric.why: The rower expends effort against the water even though the boat remains at rest relative to the shore.
rubric.description: States that the man is doing work while rowing.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for answering yes and identifying that work is done against the water or on the water.

rubric.why: Work is done because the rowing force causes displacement of the water.
rubric.description: Explains the force and displacement involved.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that the oars exert a force on water and move it, despite the boat having no displacement relative to the shore.

modelAnswer: Yes. The man does work against the water while rowing.
The oars exert a force on the water and move it backward; the boat can nevertheless remain at rest relative to the shore.

items.followUp: Define pressure and write its SI unit.

rubric.why: Force describes a push or pull acting on a body.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying force as a push or pull.

rubric.why: Pressure is the force acting normally per unit area.
rubric.description: Defines pressure and distinguishes it from force.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that pressure is force per unit area.

modelAnswer: Force is a push or pull that can change or tend to change the state of motion or shape of a body.
Pressure is the normal force acting per unit area of a surface: P = F/A.
Force is measured in newtons, whereas pressure is measured in pascals (N/m²).

items.followUp: State Pascal’s principle and describe how it helps a hydraulic lift raise a heavy load.

rubric.why: This is the principle on which hydraulic brakes operate.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that pressure applied to an enclosed liquid is transmitted undiminished in all directions.

rubric.why: The transmitted pressure operates the brake pistons and applies the brakes.
rubric.description: Connects the principle to the automobile brake system.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that pressure in the liquid is transmitted to the brake pistons, which press the brake shoes or pads against the wheel.

modelAnswer: The hydraulic brake system works on Pascal’s principle: pressure applied to an enclosed liquid is transmitted undiminished in all directions.
The pressure is transmitted through the brake fluid to the pistons at the wheels, forcing the brake shoes or pads against the wheels.

items.followUp: Name the SI temperature scale and state the freezing point of water on it.

rubric.why: Celsius and Fahrenheit are commonly used temperature scales.
rubric.description: Names the Celsius and Fahrenheit scales.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming Celsius and Fahrenheit.

rubric.why: Kelvin is the SI temperature scale.

modelAnswer: The main temperature scales are Celsius (centigrade), Fahrenheit and Kelvin.
Kelvin is the SI scale of temperature.
